20.46: And so it came to pass, that all that were slain of Benjamin in divers places, were five and twenty thousand fighting men, most valiant for war.
20.47: And there remained of all the number of Benjamin only six hundred men that were able to escape, and flee to the wilderness: and they abode in the rock Remmon four months.
20.48: But the children of Israel returning, put all the remains of the city to the sword, both men and beasts, and all the cities and villages of Benjamin were consumed with devouring flames.

21.1: Now the children of Israel had also sworn in Maspha, saying: None of us shall give of his daughters to the children of Benjamin to wife.
21.2: And they all came to the house of God in Silo, and abiding before him till the evening, lifted up their voices, and began to lament and weep, saying:
21.3: O Lord God of Israel, why is so great an evil come to pass in thy people, that this day one tribe should be taken away from among us?
21.4: And rising early the next day, they built an altar: and offered there holocausts, and victims of peace, and they said:
21.5: Who is there among all the tribes of Israel that came not up with the army of the Lord? for they had bound themselves with a great oath, when they were in Maspha, that whosoever were wanting should be slain.
21.6: And the children of Israel being moved with repentance for their brother Benjamin, began to say: One tribe is taken away from Israel.
21.7: Whence shall they take wives? For we have all in general sworn, not to give our daughters to them.
21.8: Therefore they said: Who is thereof all the tribes of Israel, that came not up to the Lord to Maspha. And behold the inhabitants of Jabes Galaad were found not to have been in that army.
21.9: (At that time also when they were in Silo, no one of them was found there.)
21.10: So they sent ten thousand of the most valiant men, and commanded them, saying: Go and put the inhabitants of Jabes Galaad to the sword, with their wives and their children.
21.11: And this is what you shall observe: Every male, and all women that have known men, you shall kill, but the virgins you shall save.
21.12: And there were found of Jabes Galaad four hundred virgins, that had not known the bed of a man, and they brought them to the camp Silo, into the land of Chanaan.
21.13: And they sent messengers to the children of Benjamin, that were in the rock Remmon, and commanded them to receive them in peace.
21.14: And the children of Benjamin came at that time, and wives were given them of the daughters of Jabes Galaad: but they found no others, whom they might give in like manner.
21.15: And all Israel was very sorry, and repented for the destroying of one tribe out of Israel.
21.16: And the ancients said: What shall we do with the rest, that have not received wives? for all the women in Benjamin are dead.
21.17: And we must use all care, and provide with great diligence, that one tribe be not destroyed out of Israel.
21.18: For as to our own daughters we cannot give them, being bound with an oath and a curse, whereby we said: Cursed be he that shall give Benjamin any of his daughters to wife.
21.19: So they took counsel, and said: Behold there is a yearly solemnity of the Lord in Silo, which is situate on the north of the city of Bethel, and on the east side of the way, that goeth from Bethel to Sichem, and on the south of the town of Lebona.
21.20: And they commanded the children of Benjamin, and said: Go, and lie hid in the vineyards,
21.21: And when you shall see the daughters of Silo come out, as the custom is, to dance, come ye on a sudden out of the vineyards, and catch you every man his wife among them, and go into the land of Benjamin.
21.22: And when their fathers and their brethren shall come, and shall begin to complain against you, and to chide, we will say to them: Have pity on them for they took them not away as by the right of war or conquest, but when they asked to have them, you gave them not, and the fault was committed on your part.
21.23: And the children of Benjamin did, as they had been commanded: and according to their number, they carried off for themselves every man his wife of them that were dancing: and they went into their possession and built up their cities, and dwelt in them.
21.25: The children of Israel also returned by their tribes, and families, to their dwellings. In those days there was no king in Israel: but every one did that which seemed right to himself.

quotes.quote: "Awake, Awake, Deborah!" Increase righteousness, establish the people, arise for the glory of God and the salvation of the people. "Gathering strength, arise Barak!" Arise and establish [the people] as was said to Moses, "Stand by me." David likewise said, "Our feet stand in your courts, O Jerusalem." "He set my feet upon the rock." Therefore, gathering strength, arise and say, "I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me!" "You are my strength and my song, O Lord." But also you, Deborah, strengthen Barak. For the saints also give courage to us in the power of the Lord, instructing our souls against our enemies. But every mind should be held captive to the obedience of Christ. And if, Deborah, you should fall in your work, like what happened to Jonathan [when he tasted the honey], may your soul be strengthened by the sweet taste of prophecy.

And are you not amazed at Manoah the Judge of yore... the one being unable to endure the sight even of one in whom was a representation of God; and saying, "We are undone, O wife, we have seen God;" speaking as though even a vision of God could not be grasped by human beings, let alone the Nature of God.

Satan the tyrant outwitted Samson with a woman,
the same tyrant outwitted Adam with a woman:
Samson had to grind at the mill, Adam had to labor wearily on the soil;
Samson prayed to be released,
whereas we pray to grow old in our misery.
Blessed is he who delivered Samson, releasing him from the grinding.
Samson is a type of the death of Christ the high priest:
Samson's death returns prisoners to their towns,
whereas the High Priest's death has returned us to our heritage.

Just as those who travel about in the pathless desert tremble at serpents on the ground, and those who travel on the pathways are also terrified of vipers that hide on the paths, so were the Philistines, who traveled on paths and in the pathless desert, terrified of Samson. "To bite the horse's heels and throw its rider backward." It was during the great famine, which God had brought upon the Philistines, that Samson burned their crops by means of foxes, for fire was carried on their bodies like a rider on its horse. Then the Philistines keeled over from lack of bread and then fell backwards from lack of nourishment.

People imitate those who do good deeds, therefore, not out of love for these good deeds but because of their utility.… The king of Moab took note of Jephthah. But, because it was his firstborn and a human being rather than an animal that he killed, God took pity on him, since he did it in affliction and not through love. In the case of Jephthah, if it had been one of his servants who had been first to encounter him, he would have killed him. The Scriptures do not seem to pass judgment on this vow and its fulfillment as it does quite clearly in the case of Abraham, when he was ordered to sacrifice his son and did so. Rather the Scriptures seem to have only recorded the matter and left it to the reader to evaluate, just as in the case of Judah, Jacob's son, who in ignorance lay with his daughter-in-law but committed fornication by the very act, because he thought her to be a prostitute. The Scriptures never approve nor disapprove of the act explicitly but let the matter stand, to be evaluated and contemplated after consulting the righteousness and law of God. Therefore, the Scriptures of God do not offer any comment in either the vow or its fulfillment, so that our mind might be put to work to pass judgment on this matter and so that we might now say that such a vow displeased God and led to the punishment that his only…

As regards to the fact that Jephthah sacrificed his daughter to God as a whole burnt offering, these are the facts: he had vowed that if he were to obtain the victory, he would offer as a whole burnt offering whoever would come out of his house and meet him; because he had vowed this and won the battle and his daughter had been the one to meet him first, he fulfilled his vow. This event has become a great and rather difficult question to settle both for some who investigate the matter with piety and genuinely seek to know what this passage means and for some who out of ignorant impiety oppose the Holy Scriptures and call this a horrible misdeed that the God of the law and prophets would have delighted in sacrifices, yes, even human sacrifices. First let us reply to their calumnies by noting that the whole burnt offerings of cattle did not delight the God of the law and the prophets—or…

But we rightly ask whether human sacrifices must have foreshadowed future events.… But if this were true, this type of sacrifice would not displease God. But in fact the Scriptures themselves clearly testify that human sacrifices displease him. For when God wanted and commanded all the firstborn to belong to him and to be his, he nonetheless wanted the firstborn of humankind to be redeemed by their parents, so that they would not entrust their firstborn children to God through immolation.…Now clearly God loves and rewards those sacrifices when a just man endures injustice and struggles for the truth even to the point of death or when he is killed by enemies whom he has offended for righteousness' sake, as he has returned them good for evil, that is, love instead of hatred.… In imitation of Abel, thousands of martyrs have struggled for the truth to the point of death and have been…

Now, judges were established over them from the time they took over the promised land and before the monarchy began. And even during this era, the children of iniquity, that is, foreign foes, afflicted them, for we read they had now peace, now war. Even so, you can find periods of peace in the age of the judges longer than that of Solomon, who reigned forty years. Specifically, under the judge named Ehud, there were eighty years of peace.

You may read that it was possible for the nations to be exterminated at once out of the land which was given to the children of Israel, and yet that God willed it to be gradually effected. And one may meet with a thousand other incidents, the past or the future possibility of which we might readily admit, and yet be unable to produce any proofs of their having ever really happened. Accordingly, it would not be right for us to deny the possibility of a man's living without sin, on the ground that amongst men none can be found except Him who is in His nature not man only, but also God, in whom we could prove such perfection of character to have existed.
quotes.source_title: ON THE SPIRIT AND THE LETTER 1

quotes.quote: Like the famed Samson, whose power lay in the strength of his hair, whose locks were endowed with sacred might, he must throttle and bring low the lion by means of the strong arms of prayers and pluck the sweet fruit of notable victory from its dead mouth.But this triumph must be a lesson to him not to make alliances with foreigners. That woman of another race I interpret as the law of the flesh, so wily with its alluring nets. If this law proves stronger than the law of the mind, it will drag him into the dominion of sin. The evil counsel of its pleasant words weakens with its deceitful guile the male spirit. It blinds the eyes of the mind and shaves the head; it plunders and disarms faith. I would not have our boy a Samson in this respect, becoming involved in a love encounter immediately followed by captivity, enervation and blindness, even though the strong Samson later recovered…

Since sacred Scripture can be understood and interpreted in many ways as a pearl, Christ himself is not unfittingly regarded as the lion.… But he was victorious in his triumph over the devil through his death on the cross. Indeed, he is both the lion and the lion's cub: a lion because equal to the Father; the lion's cub because the Son of the Father who was killed by his own will and rose again by his own power. Of him it is written: "Who will disturb him?" Voluntarily offering his father the sacrifice of his body for us, he who is most high forever takes up the life which he himself had laid down, as he testifies. That Samson says, "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness," is fittingly applied to Christ. By his teaching he both chews over the spiritual food of his honey and in his promises gives it to us. In still another way this can be understood…

Then follow the words "Samson was angry because a friend married his wife." This friend prefigured all heretics. It is a great mystery, my brothers. Heretics who divide the church have wanted to marry the wife of the Lord and carry her away. By departing from the church and the Gospels, they attempt through adulterous wickedness to seize the church, that is, the body of Christ, as their portion. For this reason that faithful servant and friend of the Lord's bride says, "I betrothed you to one spouse, that I might present you a chaste virgin to Christ." Moreover, through the zeal of faith and a rebuke he touches the person of his wicked companion: "And I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the truth which is in Christ Jesus." Who are the companions, that is, the heretical deserters who want to seize the Lord's spouse, unless Donatus, Arius,…

Now, although Gideon was brave and confident, still he sought fuller proofs of victory from the Lord, saying, "If indeed you are going to save Israel through me, as you promised, O Lord, I am putting this woolen fleece on the threshing floor. If dew comes on the fleece, while all the ground is dry, I shall know that you will save the people through me, as you promised." That is what took place. Afterwards, he added that the second time dew should pour over all the ground and only the fleece be dry; and so it happened. The dew on the fleece was faith in Judea, for the words of God descend as dew; for this reason Moses says, "May my discourse be awaited like the rain, and my words descend like the dew." Thus, when the whole world was dried up from the unproductive heat of Gentile superstition, then there was the dew of a heavenly visitation upon the fleece, that is, in Judea. However,…

When Gideon, the son of Joash, was beating the grain of wheat with a rod under an oak tree, he merited to hear an angel promise that he would deliver God's people from the power of their enemies. It is no wonder that he was chosen for a special grace, when by the predestined mystery of the future incarnation he was even then seated under the shade of the cross of holy and venerable wisdom. He was bringing the tangible grains of a fruitful field out of their concealment, separating choice holy men from the rubbish of useless chaff. Putting aside the superfluities of the old man and his actions by treating them with the rod of experienced truth, they are assembled in the church as in a winepress. The church is the winepress of the eternal fountain in which abounds the fruit of the heavenly vine.

Now when Samson destroyed a thousand men with a jawbone from the body of an ass, the Gentiles were prefigured in the ass; for thus Scripture speaks concerning both Jews and Gentiles: "An ox knows its owner, and an ass its master's manger." Before the coming of Christ all the Gentiles were torn to pieces by the devil and lay scattered like dry bones from the ass's body, but when Christ the true Samson came, he seized them all in his holy hands. He restored them by the hands of his power, and with them overcame his and our adversaries. Thus, we who had given our members to the devil before so that he might kill us, were seized by Christ and became instruments of justice unto God.

Let us see further what kind of a parable Samson proposed to the strangers. "Out of the eater came forth food," he said, "and out of the strong came forth sweetness." This parable was revealed, carried to friends and solved. Samson was defeated. If he was a just man, the fact is well hidden and the justice of the man is deep down. For since he is read to have been overcome by the flattery of a woman and went in to a harlot, his merits seem to totter in the eyes of those who do not understand so well the secrets of truth. Indeed, he is commanded by a precept of the Lord to take the harlot as his wife. Perhaps we can say that in the Old Testament this was not blameworthy or disgraceful, seeing that whatever was said or done was a matter of prophecy.

As to the question implied in the words "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness," what else does it signify but Christ rising from the dead? Truly, out of the eater, that is, from death which devours and consumes all things, came forth that food which said, "I am the bread that has come down from heaven." The Gentiles were converted and received the sweetness of life from him whom human iniquity loaded with bitterness and offered bitter vinegar and gall as a drink. Thus, from the mouth of the dead lion, that is, from the death of Christ who lay down and slept like the lion, there proceeded a swarm of bees, that is, of Christians. When Samson said, "If you had not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle," this heifer is the church which had the secrets of our faith revealed to her by her husband. By the teaching and preaching of…

Now let us see what Samson did when he was injured by his friend in the person of his wife. He took foxes, that is, adulterous friends of whom it is said in the Canticle of Canticles, "Catch us the foxes, the little foxes that damage the vineyards." What does it mean, "catch"? It means seize, convict, repress them, lest the vines of the church be destroyed. What else does it mean to catch foxes, except to convict heretics with the authority of the divine law, to fasten and fetter them with the testimony of holy Scripture as with chains? Samson caught the foxes and put torches of fire on their tails after they were coupled. What do the tails of the foxes tied together signify? What are foxes' tails except the results of heresy (for their first appearance is flattering and deceitful) bound fast, that is, condemned and dragging fire in their trail? Moreover, they destroy the fruits and…

Although all the nations in the surrounding country were subject to king David, still God did not allow the Jebusites to be destroyed entirely, as he himself says elsewhere: "I for my part will not clear away for them any more of the nations. Through them the Israelites were to be made to prove whether they would fear me." For this reason the prophet said to David, "Go up, and build an altar to the Lord in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite." That pagan king represented the people of the Gentiles. Notice, brothers, that no place in the land of the Jews was found worthy for the altar of the Lord to be built; but in the land of the Gentiles a place is chosen where the angel is seen and the altar of the Lord is built, and thus the wrath of the almighty Lord is appeased. Then already was prefigured the fact that in the hearts of the Jews no worthy place could be found to offer…

The strength which Samson possessed, dearly beloved, came from the grace of God rather than by nature, for if he had been naturally strong his power would not have been taken away when his hair was cut. Where, then, was that most powerful strength, except in what the Scripture says: "The Spirit of the Lord walked with him"? Therefore, his strength belonged to the Spirit of the Lord. In Samson was the vessel, but the fullness was in the Spirit. A vessel can be filled and emptied. Moreover, every vessel has its perfection from something else, and so in Paul grace was commended when he was called a vessel of election.

When Samson went in to the harlot, he was impure if he did so without reason, but if he did so as a prophet it is a mystery. If he did not enter in order to lie with the woman, perhaps he did so because of a mystery. We do not read that he was intimate with her.… See how it is not recorded in Scripture that he was united to the harlot whom he had visited, but it is written that he slept.… He took away the city gates through which he had gone in to the harlot and carried them to a mountain. What does this mean? Hell and love for a woman Scripture joins together; the house of the harlot was an image of hell. It is rightly considered as hell, for it rejects no one but draws to itself all who enter. At this point we recognize the actions of our Redeemer. After the synagogue to which he had come was separated from him through the devil, they shaved his head, that is, they crucified him on…

Many of the fathers have spoken a great deal about this lion, beloved brothers, and all of them have said what is fitting and in accord with the facts. Some have said that the lion prefigured Christ our Lord. Truly, this is very appropriate, for to us Christ is a lion in whose mouth we found the food of honey after his death. What is sweeter than the Word of God? Or what is stronger than his right hand? In whose mouth after death is there food and bees, except his in whose word is the good of our salvation and the congregation of the Gentiles? The lion can further be understood as the Gentiles who believed. First, it was a body of vanity, but is now the body of Christ in which the apostles like bees stored the honey of wisdom gathered from the dew of heaven and the flowers of divine grace. Thus, food came out of the mouth of the one who died; because nations which were as fierce as…

Now what does it mean that Samson possessed strength in his hair? Notice this carefully, too, brothers. He did not have strength in his hand, his foot, his chest, not even in his head, but in his hair. What is hair? If we perceive it, the apostle answers us after being questioned, "Hair is a covering"; and Christ had strength in a covering, when the shadows of the old law protected him. For this reason the hair of Samson was a covering, since it was seen and understood in Christ at different times. What does it mean that Samson's secret was betrayed and his head was shaved? The law was despised and Christ suffered. They would not have killed Christ if they had not contemned the law, for they knew that it was not right for them to kill him. They told the judge, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death." Samson's head was shaved, the secrets were exposed, the covering was removed;…

What was the meaning of Samson? If I say he signified Christ, it seems to me that I speak the truth. However, the thought immediately occurs to anyone who reflects: Was Christ overcome by the flattery of a woman? How is Christ understood to have gone in to a prostitute? Then, again, when did Christ have his head uncovered or his hair shaved, himself robbed of courage, bound, blinded and mocked? Watch, faithful soul. Notice why it is Christ, not only what Christ did, but also what he suffered. What did he do? He worked as a strong man and suffered as a weak one. In the one person I understand both qualities; I see the strength of the Son of God and the weakness of the Son of man. Moreover, when the Scriptures extol him, Christ is entire, both head and body. Just as Christ is the head of the church, so the church is his body; and in order that it might not be alone, it is the whole Christ…

Furthermore, the fact that after Samson's hair grew again he recovered his former strength and seizing the pillars destroyed the house of his enemies together with its builders, is also seen today in the case of some sinners. If they destroy their vices by repentance and provide a place for virtue, the likeness and figure of Samson is fulfilled in them. Then is accomplished in them what is written concerning Samson: "Those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his lifetime." It is true, brothers. A greater number of sins is destroyed by repentance than is known to be overcome at a time when one seems to be free from offenses. Now we should not notice with indifference that at the death of Samson all his enemies were killed. Thus, may our adversaries also be destroyed at our death. Brothers, the apostle says, "Mortify your members, which are on earth: lust,…

Now that splendor which was restored in Samson and was covered at his death I think fits every servant of Christ. If someone is overtaken by some sin and in a salutary manner has recourse to the remedies of repentance, with the restoration of grace there returns the face of a good conscience, like the hair which grew again. Thus, it becomes possible for the merits of faith like very strong muscles of courage to attack and overthrow the enemy's pillars which support the hostile house. What are these pillars of the enemy's house except our sins upon which the house of the devil rests, where he feasts as victor and mocks our minds if they have been captivated? Therefore, we eject this enemy from his house by the destruction and death of our flesh. Our enemy is enclosed within us; he daily wages an internal war inside. As long as we sometimes assent to him, in accord with the evil agreement…

"Therefore his enemies brought him to play the buffoon before them." Notice here an image of the cross. Samson extends his hands spread out to the two columns as to the two beams of the cross. Moreover, by his death he overcame his adversaries, because his sufferings became the death of his persecutors. For this reason Scripture concludes as follows: "Those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his lifetime." This mystery was clearly fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ, for at his death he completed our redemption which he had by no means publicly announced during his life: who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

Although we had been dried up because of lack of the dew of God's grace, we merited to be changed into fountains and rivers. At that time Samson prayed and a fountain issued from the jawbone. This fact is clearly fulfilled in us, for the Lord himself said, "He who believes in me, from within him there shall flow rivers of living water."

In the relics of the saints the Lord Christ has provided us with saving fountains which in many ways pour out benefactions and gush with fragrant ointment. And let no one disbelieve. For, if by the will of God water poured out of the precipitous living rock in the desert, and for the thirsty Samson from the jawbone of an ass, is it unbelievable that fragrant ointment should flow from the relics of the martyrs? Certainly not, at least for such as know the power of God and the honor which the saints have from him.

Therefore to God alone appertains worship, and this the very angels know, that though they excel other beings in glory, yet they are all creatures and not to be worshiped, but worship the Lord. Thus Manoah, the father of Samson, wishing to offer sacrifice to the angel, was thereupon hindered by him, saying, "Offer not to me, but to God." On the other hand, the Lord is worshiped even by the angels; for it is written: "Let all the angels of God worship him."

Our sufferings have been dreadful beyond endurance, and it is impossible to describe them in suitable terms; but in order that the dreadful nature of the events which have taken place may be more readily apprehended, I have thought it good to remind you of a history out of the Scriptures. It happened that a certain Levite was injured in the person of his wife; and, when he considered the exceeding greatness of the pollution (for the woman was a Hebrew, and of the tribe of Judah), being astounded at the outrage which had been committed against him, he divided his wife's body, as the holy Scripture relates in the book of Judges, and sent a part of it to every tribe in Israel, in order that it might be understood that an injury like this pertained not to himself only, but extended to all alike; and that if the people sympathized with him in his sufferings, they might avenge him; or if they…

We read that when God wished it clearly understood that great deeds were done by him, they were done through a few or through the lowliest, lest the work of his heavenly hand be attributed to human strength. In this way the leader Sisera, before whom the Hebrew army trembled, was laid low by a woman.

Against the Midianites, also, who, as the book of Judges relates, had filled all places like locusts, Gideon was ordered to lead a few men into battle. It was not that he did not have many in his army, but that he was forbidden to lead many into battle, lest the multitude might claim for itself some share of the victory. Hence, when he had gathered thirty thousand armed fighters, the Lord spoke thus to him: "the people with you are too many, and the Midianites shall not be given into their hands."What happened next? He left only three hundred fighters to the man who was about to fight against countless thousands of barbarians. Indeed, he ordered the line of soldiers to be reduced to the smallest number in order that their fewness would not permit them to realize any credit from the prosecution of the divinely waged war. Why the Lord acted thus, he himself very clearly stated, saying,…

Rightly, then, do we compare Mary with fleece—she who conceived the Lord in such a way that she absorbed him with her whole body; nor did she undergo a rending of that same body, but she was tender in submission and firm in chastity. Rightly, I say, is Mary compared with fleece—she from whose offspring saving garments are woven for the people. Clearly Mary is fleece since from her tender womb came forth the Lamb who himself, bearing his mother's wool (that is, flesh), covers the wounds of all peoples with a soft fleece. For every wound of sin is covered with the wool of Christ, tended by the blood of Christ, and, so that it may receive health, clothed in the garment of Christ.

Let us avoid, then, brothers, let us avoid the pestilential deceits of the insidious foxes [heretics]. Let us avoid the deadly frauds of wicked persons lest, like the foxes which that famous strong man Samson once sent into the Philistines' fields, bearing torches on their tails that burned up everything with their flames, the foxes of perverse teachings in like manner either get hold of the fruits of our fields by deceitful traps or consume them by burning flames. Let us, therefore, as we read, be simple and clever—that is to say, simple as doves and clever as serpents, so that the cleverness of the serpents might protect the simplicity of the doves.

"All Midian, therefore," it says, "and Amalek and the sons of the East gathered together and went up and came upon them and pitched their camp in the valley of Jezreel." These, who wish to assail the people of God, "pitch their camp in the valleys," in low and lowly places, "in the valley," it says, "of Jezreel." Now we find that Jezreel is interpreted as "the seed of God." Do you see where the adversaries "pitch their camp"? They did not dare to go there where the "fruits of the Spirit" are seen to have already been born, but where the seed of God still lies, where the fruit has not yet come up. For he who "went out to sow" "sows the word" over every place, but hear the Lord himself saying what the seed of God is wont to suffer: "some," he says, "fell by the wayside, and the birds of heaven come and snatch it away." Which, interpreting in what follows, he himself says: "but those who…

"And the children of Israel did what was wicked before God". Almighty God, our ruler, grant that it may never happen to us that Jesus Christ, after he has risen from the dead, should again die in us. For what does it profit me if in others he lives by virtue and in me he dies by the weakness of sin? What does it profit me if in me and in my heart he does not live, and if in me he does not accomplish the works of life? What does it profit me if in another he is nourished and refreshed by good pursuits, by good faith, by good works, but in me and in my heart he is in a manner suffocated and slain by evil thoughts and unspeakable desires, by the worst pursuits? For see what Scripture adds, that: "there arose", it says, "another generation, which did not know Jesus and the great works which he did". That "generation, which did not know" the Lord "Jesus", is the one of "evil thoughts" and…

"And the children of Israel served," it says, "Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years." Observe that divine Scripture indicates even the measures of the punishment; there it says "for eight years" and here "for eighteen." Now it is certain that according to the measure of the sin and the delay of our conversion the times of chastisement too are determined.

Therefore speak in the ears of the people, saying: Whoever is timid and fearful of heart, let him return. And there returned from Mount Gilead, out of the people, twenty-two thousand men, and there remained ten thousand. Let us see, then, first, what it means that He says: "timid and fearful of heart"; for two things are named by which human frailty is convicted, that is, the "timid" and the "fearful" of heart. He may seem "timid" who at the first sight trembles at the encounter, yet is not terrified with his whole heart, but can be restored and heartened again. But the fearful man is he who, the vice as it were now taking root, is terrified by thought alone even before he sees the evils, rolling an icy dread through his limbs, so that he is unmanned not so much by the sight of evils as by the very hearing and expectation of them; and therefore He added: "fearful of heart"; for this…

But having briefly gone back over these matters from the earlier reading — that is, over the end of Ehud — let us now see what sort the beginning of Shamgar is also, who is there interpreted "stranger." For it is true that all who are men of God are strangers in this world and sojourners upon the earth, just as was also he who said that: "I am a sojourner with thee upon the earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were". And so the Holy Spirit there calls this Shamgar too a sojourner — that is, here. For what is "there" to the Holy Spirit, who is in the heavens, is "here" to us. What, then, is said of Shamgar? "He smote", it says, "the Philistines, six hundred men, with the handle — or "foot" — of a plow". I see another kind of praise in Shamgar: this one fights with a "plow". Ehud was fighting with a sword, this one with a plow. Yet this one too conquers, overcomes, and lays low the…

And after this it says: "the land had rest under him as judge for forty years." You see how bountiful is the divine clemency. "For eight years the children of Israel had served" for the offenses of many; "for forty years" they endure in peace for the righteousness of one.

But let us also consider this — where the prophecy is said to "reside" and where its place is described. "Under a palm tree," it says, "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." Prophecy has its seat "under a palm tree," because "the righteous man," says David, "will flourish like a palm tree" — through this, that prophecy leads the one instructed by its teachings to the "palm of the heavenly calling of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord." And it is said to sit "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." "Ramah" is interpreted as "heights". "Bethel," however, as "the house of God". See in what places "prophecy" is said to "reside" — between the heights and the house of God. For nothing lowly, nothing cast down, nothing base can be found near the seat of prophecy; just as Solomon likewise, describing the seat of wisdom, says of it that she either "stands at the gates…

"And then," it says, "Gideon said to God: if you save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, behold, here I am, and I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor; and if indeed dew falls upon the fleece and there is dryness upon all the earth, I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken. And it was done so." Since there are so many and innumerable signs or prodigies which Gideon could have asked from God to confirm God's promise, why did it seem good to him, after the angelic voice and the heavenly promise, to ask of God this so novel a sign? For he says: "I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor, and if there is dew upon the fleece only and dryness upon all the earth, I shall be confident that you will save Israel by my hand." And when Gideon had asked this sign of God, he obtained its fulfillment. But granted, O Gideon, that you have…

But if from this too something seems worthy of being asked by diligent hearers — namely that he is said to have "given him milk to drink" when he had asked for "water" — let us see whether perhaps, according to the mystical or allegorical laws, something of this kind can also be shown concerning this. The food of "milk" is said in the holy Scriptures to be this first moral instruction, which is delivered to beginners as though to "little ones." For at the beginnings the deep and more hidden mysteries are not at once to be delivered to disciples, but the correction of morals, the amendment of discipline, the first elements of religious conduct and of simple faith are delivered to them. This is the "milk" of the Church, these are the first elements of the "little ones" who are beginning. But this food indeed bestows life and salvation upon those who bear the purpose of advancing toward…

The Spirit, therefore, "asks" and "intercedes," but we "pray." And Joshua's words commanding the sun to stand over [Gibeon] seem to me to be an intercession also.… And in Judges, Samson in my opinion said in intercession: "Let me die with the foreigners—when he bent in his strength and the house fell upon the princes and all the people that were there." Even though it is not written that Joshua and Samson "interceded" but that they "said," nevertheless their words seem to be an "intercession," which we must judge to be different from a "prayer," if we are to give words their proper meaning.

But that also, which Gideon says: "I will place the fleece" — not just anywhere, not in a field nor in a woodland, but "on the threshing-floor" — how does it seem to you? "On the threshing-floor," where the "harvest" is: "for the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few." "I will place," he says, "the fleece" there, where the "harvest" is. What had moved the holy man Gideon, or what had seemed good to him, that he should do this? For he foresaw through the Spirit that Christ "gathers" his people "into the threshing-floor" and there cleanses him, "holding the winnowing-fan in his hand," and there separates the "chaff" from the wheat. Not without cause, therefore, did so great and such a man — of whom the holy Apostle too, writing to the Hebrews, makes mention in the catalogue of the prophets — choose the threshing-floor for placing the fleece; nor without cause did he "wring out the…

Now it is described that, when according to the admonition of Deborah — that is, of prophecy — Barak pursued Sisera the leader of the Philistines, he himself indeed could not seize him, but there met him "as he fled" a foreign woman, Jael, which woman had previously held a covenant of friendship with him; "to whom," when he had "turned aside" for the sake of hiding, he asked for water to drink, but by her "he was given milk to drink"; and when she had placed him "in hiding" and had covered him with skins, after this she drove a stake, driven in "with a mallet," through his cheeks — or "jaws" — and fixed it fast: and then, "meeting" Barak as he pursued, she "showed Sisera" "now dead" and laid low.

What, then, does all this text of the history show us of the mystery? "Jael," that foreign "woman" concerning whom prophecy said that the victory would come to pass "into the hand of a woman," holds the figure of the Church, which has been gathered from the foreign nations. Now "Jael" is interpreted as "ascent", because in truth there is no other ascent by which one may ascend to heaven except "through the Church of the manifold wisdom of God." She, therefore, is the one who, while she ascends from bodily things to spiritual and from earthly to heavenly, slays Sisera — of whom we have already said above that he holds the figure of the carnal vices and of the "animal" or "earthy" man, because Sisera is interpreted as "the sight of a horse", concerning which Scripture says: "do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." With a stake, therefore, she slays him —…

But let us see what befalls those who are handed over for their sins. "And the children of Israel made for themselves," it says, "because of the face of Midian, dens in the mountains and in the caves and in the strongholds; and it came to pass, when a man of Israel had sown, that Midian and Amalek and the sons of the East came up against them; and they came upon them and destroyed all the fruits of the land, until one came to Gaza." These things, indeed, that one suffered who was Israel according to the flesh; he sowed the land, but because he had been handed over for his sins to the enemies rising up against him, instead of crops "he reaped corruption." But as for us, who are named Israel according to the spirit, let us consider what such thing can befall us. There is a time when we sow and the enemies cannot corrupt the seeds that we sow, they cannot lie in wait for our husbandry; but…

This prophecy, therefore, first of all, it says, "sent and called Barak to herself." Now "Barak" is interpreted as "flashing". But a flashing is that which has light indeed, but not lasting; for it shines forth for a little while and ceases. This Barak, therefore, seems to me to bear the figure of the former people, who first of all was called through prophecy and invited to hear the utterances of God and to receive the gifts of the divine law — who indeed shone and flashed in the splendor of the law for a brief time, but did not long endure nor was able to obtain the continuous brightness of the light. When, therefore, Deborah had said to Barak — that is, prophecy to the former people — that: "the Lord God of Israel has commanded you, and do you go up onto Mount Tabor, and take ten thousand men" and the rest that is written, let us see what Barak, in the person of the people, answered…

"O mighty ones of the people, bless the Lord, you who have mounted upon beasts of burden". What is it "to have mounted upon a beast of burden"? This body of mine is a "beast of burden"; for it was given for the aid of the soul and for its ministry; but it is I, that is, the inner man, "who have mounted upon" this "beast of burden", to whom it is said that I should "bless the Lord". If therefore you have truly mounted upon the body and have been made superior to bodily desires, and the motions of your body are governed by the bridle of the mind and by the direction of the inner man, it is said of you that you "have mounted upon a beast of burden", that you may "bless the Lord". But what is it that follows? "You who sit upon vehicles", it says, "and shine upon she-asses". What do "shining she-asses" seem to be? For the Scripture says that "those who sit upon vehicles and upon shining…

We pass from questions to questions and from mysteries to mysteries, and while we can scarcely and with difficulty explain each of the first things, more difficult matters follow upon the difficult ones — matters which do not so much require the eloquence of human talent as they demand the inspiration of divine grace. For without doubt the hearer will ask — since indeed there is that saying of the Apostle Paul which declares: "all Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproof, for instruction which is in righteousness" — what this Scripture has in itself (which we likewise without doubt confess to be divinely inspired) that may yield to us "for instruction," that may yield "for reproof," that may yield "for discipline," that may yield "for righteousness." For what is conferred upon us from this, if we read what has just been recited — that is, that "Deborah," it says,…

But after these "twenty-two thousand departed", the divine discourse adds still further and "says to Gideon": "Still", it says, "the people are many; bring them down to the water, and there I will test them for you". As I see it, those who were first rejected had not even gone down "into the water", but were still marking themselves out as catechumens, and were so deterred by the vice of dread that they did not even go down to the saving washing: those, then, were rejected in this way. But these second ones come "to the water", that they may be tested there. And how they are tested, let us see:

Let us see, then, whether perhaps through these things we may be taught something worthy, as also from the other Scriptures, concerning the more hidden mysteries. First, this very fact that, although many men are reported to have been judges in Israel, of none of them is it said that he was a "prophet" except of "Deborah the woman." Even the very first surface of the letter itself furnishes no small consolation to the female sex in this, and it summons them, that they should by no means despair, on account of the weakness of their sex, of being able to become capable even of the grace of prophecy, but that they should understand and believe that purity of mind, not diversity of sex, merits this grace. But let us see what secret of the inner understanding also breathes forth here. "Deborah" is interpreted as "bee or speech". But we have already said in the earlier passages too that…

They, therefore, "pitch their camp in the valleys." "But the Spirit," it says, "of God strengthened Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, upon the horn of the trumpet, and called Abiezer after him." The continuity of the exposition, indeed, required a different order, but because we are now speaking not so much to comment on the Scriptures as to console the people concerning those things which have been read, we treat here and there, as they occur, of individual points. "He called," it says, "Abiezer after him," who indeed was nowhere at all. Now "Abiezer" is interpreted as "the help of my father." Therefore Gideon seems to have called upon not some man, but the help of the highest Father. Meanwhile he also sends to summon reinforcements. The peoples come together, and the whole army is gathered to Gideon.

"Arise, Deborah, arise and rouse up the ten thousands of the people". When does prophecy "arise"? Assuredly at the coming of Christ, and not only does it itself "arise", but it also "rouses up" the peoples to believe. "Lead captivity captive, O son of Abinoam". "Abinoam" is interpreted as "the answer of the father". His son is Barak. He "will take captivity" from the enemies, who has kept the answers of the heavenly Father.

But what is added after this? "And the children of Israel", it says, "added to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and Ehud was dead". Undoubtedly in these matters too there is preserved that observation which we pointed out in the preceding passages: that for the sins of the people the good leader of the people dies. For when they have been made unworthy and have "done evil in the sight of God", the man of God will be taken away from them. But perhaps our people will say: when is the Church of God without a judge? Even if the former departs, another is supplied. Perhaps we shall say something bold, yet we say what is written. Not always is the prince of the people and judge of the Church given by the judgment of God, but according as our merits demand. If our deeds are evil and we "work evil in the sight of God", princes are given to us according to our heart; and this I will prove to…

After this it says: "hear, O kings, and give ear, O satraps: to the Lord I will sing, I will sing praise to the God of Israel". "Hear", it says, "O kings". It calls "kings" those who are summoned to hear the word of God. Exult, O people of God, hearing the insignia of your nobility. You are called to hear the word of God, and you are called not as the common crowd, but as a king. For to you it has been said: "a royal priestly race, a people for acquisition". Therefore, because you are "kings", deservedly is our king Christ the Lord called "king of kings and lord of those who rule". But just as you have exulted over the title of your nobility, so ought you to learn what each of you must do to become a king. Which I will define for you thus, briefly. It makes you a king over all, if Christ reigns in you; for a king is so called from ruling. If therefore in you too the mind reigns and the…

"And the prince", it says, "of the army of Jabin was Sisera, and he himself dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles, and he had nine hundred iron chariots. And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord". In this too there is likewise kept that observation which we designated above: that the children of Israel do not know how "to cry out to the Lord", except when "they have been delivered into the hands of Jabin", or when they are afflicted through his "prince of the army, Sisera", who "had", it says, "nine hundred iron chariots", by which of course the people of stiff neck was afflicted. Now "Sisera" is interpreted "vision of a horse." For he is the "animal" and not the "spiritual" man, who sees nothing except those things which are "animal"; that is his vision, that is ever his gaze. And therefore the "animal man" and "he who is according to the flesh" always "persecutes him who is…

"And the Lord said", it says, "to Gideon: everyone who shall lap the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set him apart; and everyone who shall bend his knees to drink, you shall set him aside. And the number", it says, "of those who lapped the water in their hand or with the tongue was three hundred men, but all the rest bent their knees to drink the water. And the Lord said to Gideon: by these three hundred men who lapped I will save you and deliver Midian into your hand". In almost all the deeds of the ancients vast mysteries are signified, as we see happening also in this passage, because those who go down "to the water", that is, who come to the grace of baptism, ought not to fall down to the earth nor "bend their knees" and yield to the temptations that are to come, but to stand bravely and steadfastly, as the prophet also said: "Lift up the hands that hang down and the…

Granted, the Midianites have gathered against Israel, they who are interpreted as "outside judgment." Granted, these have gathered against Israel, who are outside the judgment of God and "who have sinned outside the law and will perish outside the law." Granted, Amalek too has gathered, who himself is likewise interpreted as "a people that licks up." Granted, this nation too, earthly and given over to the belly and the gullet, has come to make war — a carnal Israel against the spiritual Israel. But what is this, that even the "sons of the East" are mingled with them and are said to come with them to make war on Israel? For my hearer says to me: if it had been written that the "sons" of the West "gathered with them," I would ask nothing; for you would tell me by the laws of allegory that the sons of the West are the sons of darkness, and that they join themselves to those nations,…

Vast was the multitude that had been gathered against Israel, so great that for its number it was compared to "locusts". "And their camels", it says, "were like the sand which is beyond number upon the shore of the sea". Let us see, then, how so countless a multitude of enemies could be overcome: there went out, it says, thirty-two thousand armed men from the sons of Israel with Gideon to fight against all that multitude. And God gave answer to Gideon, saying: "The multitude that is with you is great". And what if "the multitude is great"? Does not a more numerous army in wars afford safer defenses? By no means, He says, for divine battles are not carried out as human ones are. The work of the divine power is not made illustrious if it is propped up by human supports, because: "a king is not made safe by the greatness of his own power". Therefore, lest perhaps Israel should boast and in…

But let us see what this "ambidextrous" judge does. "The children of Israel sent," it says, "gifts to Eglon king of the Moabites by the hand of Ehud"; "and Ehud made himself a sword sharpened on both sides, of the length of an extended palm, and girded it to himself upon his right thigh." You see that everything is right-handed which this "ambidextrous" "Ehud" carries out: he is right-handed both in hands and right-handed in feet. For he carries the sword on his right thigh, that he may come to the "king of Moab" and slay him. We had said above that these whom God is said to raise up for the salvation of the people and for the delivering of the children of Israel — the saviors or judges — bear the image of certain princes from the "heavenly host" and of the supernal powers, which God sends forth for the aid of those who cry out to him with their whole heart and by the conversion of…

The death of Jesus too has been read to us. That he, indeed, "the son of Nun", "died" is no wonder; for he paid what was owed to nature. But since we had undertaken to refer these things, which were read concerning the son of Nun, to our Lord Jesus Christ, we must see how it may fittingly be said even of him that: "Jesus died". I think — speaking this too, however, according to the authority of Scripture — that in some Jesus lives, but in some he has "died". In Paul Jesus lives, and in Peter, and in all those who can deservedly say: "and now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me". And again he says: "for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain". In such men as these, therefore, Jesus is deservedly said to "live". But in whom has "Jesus died"? In those, without doubt, who by repenting often and again transgressing are said as it were to insult the death of Jesus; concerning…

The fourth song is in the book of Judges, concerning which it is written: "And Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying: When the leaders in Israel began, in the purpose of the people, bless ye the Lord. Hear, O kings, and give ear," and the rest. But she who sings these things ought to be a bee, whose work is such that both kings and ordinary folk use it for health. For Deborah, who sings this song, is interpreted "a bee," and Barak too along with her: and Barak is interpreted "lightning-flash." And this song is sung after victory, because no one can sing what is perfect until he has conquered his adversaries. So, finally, in the song itself it is said: "Arise, arise, Deborah, rouse up the thousands of the people. Arise, arise, sing a song, arise, Barak." But concerning these things too you will find matters more fully discussed in those little discourses which we…
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

quotes.quote: "The land rests" as long as sin rests. But the land is said to be moved—that is, those who dwell in the land—when sins have begun to move and disturb the souls of men. And this is why what the present reading now contains has been written. "And the land rested," it says, "for forty years. And the children of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years. And Midian prevailed over Israel." So then, as long as there was righteousness in the land—that is, in those who dwelt in the land—"the land" is said "to have rested"; but when iniquity increased and "they did evil in the sight of the Lord," then, it says, "the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years." Nor are the Midianites said to have prevailed over the people of the Lord as long as the people kept the Lord's precepts. But when it began to…

"And it served", it says, "the Baalim, and they forsook the Lord God of their fathers". These things indeed the ancients did, but since the things that are written are said to have been written not for their sake, but "for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come", let us see whether these things may seem to be said in greater part of us than of them. And do you wish to see that not by me, but by the Apostle these things are expounded as being about us? Hear himself what he says: "but in Elijah what does the Scripture say, how he pleads with God against Israel? Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what does the divine answer say to him? I have left for myself seven thousand men, who have not bent the knee to Baal" — and he adds: "so therefore", he says, "also at this present time a remnant…

Therefore "they provoked the Lord to anger, and forsook the Lord, they worshipped Baal and Astarte. And the Lord was angry with fury against Israel, and delivered them into the hands of plunderers". As long as one serves God, he is not "delivered into the hands of plunderers". But when he has "forsaken the Lord" and has begun to serve his own passions, then it is said of him that: "God delivered them into passions of ignominy", and again: "he delivered them into a reprobate mind, that they should do those things which are not fitting". Why? Because "they are filled", he says, "with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice", and all the rest that are named — just as here too now, since "they served", it says, "and adored the Baalim and Astarte, God delivered them into the hands of plunderers; and it came to pass in the hands of their enemies". For these things, as I have already…

The remaining sacrifices, of which those relating to the law are a symbol, are akin to this sacrifice. But in addition, the other sacrifices akin to this sacrifice seem to me to be the shedding of the blood of the noble martyrs. It was not in vain that the disciple John saw them standing beside the heavenly altar. "But who is wise, that he shall understand these things? Or intelligent, and he shall know them?"3Now comprehend, even if to a limited extent, the more spiritual sense of such sacrifices which cleanse those for whom they are offered; one must understand the sense of the sacrifice of the daughter of Jephthah who was offered as a burnt offering because of the vow of him who conquered the children of Ammon. She who was offered as a burnt offering consented to this vow, for, when her father said, "I have opened my mouth to the Lord against you," she said to him, "And if you have…
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.276-78

quotes.quote: But what is said after this? "And Othniel," it says, "the son of Kenaz, died." I see a perilous matter. "Othniel died." Why? Because the people was now unworthy to have such a judge. Then in what follows, after he had died, it says: "and the children of Israel added," it says, "to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel." Consider that, because they were now unworthy to have such a leader, for that reason the good judge is taken away from them. And because they "did evil in the sight of the Lord," there is stirred up against them a most wicked enemy, "Eglon king of Moab." You see that our sins supply strength to our enemies, and that, when we "do evil in the sight of the Lord" and transgress, then our adversaries "are strengthened by the Lord," then strength is given to the contrary powers. Whether you seek this according to the…

"O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". This is the voice of the faithful, who confess simply that their enemies are stronger, against whom is our struggle and battle, because "our battle is not against flesh and blood" — otherwise our adversary would not be stronger — but since "our wrestling is against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world and against the spiritual forces of wickedness", therefore the prophet says: "O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". For how should this so great force of spirits not be far more powerful than human frailty? But in this God "helps our weakness", in that the Apostle says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ". These powers, then, are indeed stronger than we; but again, "Christ", who is in us and "strengthens" us, is stronger than all, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages…

But since we do not undertake to expound the continuation of the song point by point, let us at least, skipping over the sequence of the reading, see what it means where it says: "my heart is toward the things that have been appointed for this Israel". This seems to me to be what it means: my heart and my soul and my sense and my whole mind is bent toward that and looks forward to that "which has been appointed" and which has been prepared "for Israel"; I look forward with my whole mind to that which is to come. For if I bend my mind toward that, all the things that are in this world "I will count as dung, that I may gain Christ", who "has prepared" all those things "which eye has not seen and ear has not heard nor has ascended into the heart of man, for those who love him". "My heart", therefore, it says, "is stretched out toward those things". For I no longer bear a human heart, nor…

"There they shall render acts of righteousness to the Lord". That sacrifice is acceptable to the Lord which is offered to God in righteousness and equity, and therefore it is said: "the just have been strengthened in Israel". Among the other nations, indeed, those who are stronger in bodily might are called "mighty" in battle; but in Israel, those who are more just are themselves called the more powerful in wars, because righteousness, even if it be weak in strength, conquers, whereas unrighteousness, even if it have many and strong defenders, is overcome. So therefore in this nation of ours, that is, in the people of God, either through righteousness we overcome or through unrighteousness we are conquered.

What, then, does Scripture say concerning this Othniel? After it had said that "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord," "the Spirit of the Lord came," it says, "upon Othniel, and he judged Israel." Do you suppose there is among us anyone who so "sends forth to the Lord a cry" so strong and so just that he is worthy to be heard, and the people deserve to receive a judge — and such a judge, one whom the "Spirit of God" may fill, that he may be able to hold to right judgment? Whence also the book itself is called the book of Judges, and in it are described the judges who judged the people. For just as other books are called the books of Kings, or of Kingdoms, in which is described each of the kings, how he reigned and what he did, so also in this little book the deeds of the Judges are recounted, and there is described not only whatever was done rightly and usefully by them, but…

The reader of the present lesson was reading it thus: "and the people feared the Lord all the days of Joshua", but we have: "and the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of their elders, who were of longer days after Joshua". We must therefore understand that each one of us secures it for himself, whether he be in good days or in evil, and whether he have "the days of Joshua" — that is, the days of the righteous — or have the days of the impious. For if we understand "the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world", and offer it our souls to enlighten, or if "the sun of righteousness" rise upon us and "enlighten the world" of our soul, then we too have "the days of Jesus" Christ, the days of salvation. But if anyone offers his soul to receive that light which "shall be extinguished", the light contrary to the truth, and is enlightened by it,…

Now he calls Othniel the Savior, who is interpreted as "the time of God for me". Through this Othniel, therefore, that former people was snatched from the servitude of humiliation, and peace was restored to the people — the peace which pride and the various crimes of the people had for a while put to flight. But since we have said that a certain Cushan-rishathaim can be understood spiritually, both as a king and as one of the adversaries and a prince among the "airy powers," so it seems to me consequent that this Othniel too, who was raised up to deliver the people, is some one of the "heavenly host" and of the archangelic troops which "are sent as a help to those who obtain the inheritance of salvation"; and there are saving angels who are designated under the figure either of Othniel or of Ehud, because, as we have often shown, we are not only assailed by the contrary powers, but the…

Yet how do these fight? "Pitchers", it says, they carry, "and lamps and horn trumpets in their hands", and thus, it says, they come against those countless multitudes of the enemy, among whom were "camels like the sand of the sea". And when they had come to the battle, "with the horn trumpets", it says, "they sounded". And they let go the "pitchers" from their hands, and "they were shattered". But then, snatching up the lamps, they rush upon the adversaries, and at the same time crash out with the trumpets. See how the chosen soldiers of God fight with lamps. For thus had Christ armed them, saying: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning", and again: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven". With such lamps kindled, then, it befits the soldiers of Christ to fight, shining with the light of their works and…

When "the children of Israel did evil in the sight of God, and forgot the Lord their God," and, forsaking him, "served the Baalim and the groves" of the nations, then, "storing up wrath for themselves," they "were handed over," by the just judgment of God, "into the hands of their enemies," according to what the present reading has declared: "into the hands," it says, "of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia." Now Cushan-rishathaim is interpreted as "their humiliation". They "were handed over," therefore, "into the hands" of him who would humiliate them. And because they themselves were acting impiously against the Most High upon the high places of the mountains, for that reason they are handed over by him into humiliation. But I would not have you think that this divine providence was directed only toward the ancients — namely, that it handed over those who impiously exalted…

Now therefore let us see what these do who are handed over on account of sin and set in tribulation. Precisely that which is written: "and they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation, and he delivered them out of their distresses." "And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds asunder." But each one of us also — even if he be small, even if he be the least, even if he enjoy no dignity in the world — can be afflicted with the vice of pride; and nothing is so foul nor so execrable, as Scripture says, as "a poor man who is proud and a rich man who is a liar." Sometimes, however, this disease of pride penetrates not only the poor of the common people, but strikes even the priestly and Levitical order itself. You may find sometimes even among us certain persons — we who are set as an example of humility and placed in the circle of the altar like…

Sisera, together with his army and his "iron chariots", with which he was assailing the people of God, was overcome, as prophecy had foretold would come to pass through Deborah. And after the victory was accomplished "by the hand of a woman", Deborah is recorded to have sung this song as, so to speak, the very praise of that victory. But if we remember the things that were said in the earlier passages — namely, according to the mystical pattern, what figure Deborah is, and Barak likewise, what image the woman Jael holds, who alone cast down the adversary of God's people, what image Sisera himself is, who was laid low by a foreign woman through the power of wood — we understand that all these are sacraments which are brought to completion in the last times and at the end of the age through the Church, and that in this song is described, as it were, its triumph-song, that is, the praise…

"In the beginning, when the princes were in Israel, in the free wills of the people, bless the Lord". The blessing, he says, with which "we bless the Lord", let it be "in the outset of the princes in Israel", and then afterwards also "in the free wills of the people". For example, when we first begin to come to the worship of God, when we receive the beginning of the word of God and of heavenly teaching, these beginnings must be taken up by us from the "princes of Israel". And by "princes of Israel", that is, of the Christian people, I think we must understand the "angels", whom the Lord says are present to each "least one" in the Church, who are also said "always to see the face of the Father who is in heaven". They therefore are the "princes", and from them our beginnings must be taken. For example, if a boy goes to school, he is indeed received by the master and becomes the pupil of…

To the rule of Ehud the ambidextrous is joined the rule of Shamgar. But let us see how Ehud, who is interpreted "praise," brought his rule to a close. The narrative has taught us those things which are written concerning Eglon the king, how this most wise Ehud, using a certain artifice and, so to speak, a cunning but praiseworthy deception, slew Eglon the tyrant, who is interpreted "whirling" or "of the wheel-track." Such, then, ought the judges of our people also to be, as was that Ehud who is interpreted "praise," so that they may cut down all the whirling motions and wheel-tracks of the evil path and destroy the king of the Midianites. Now the Midianites are interpreted "flowing" or "outpouring." Who, then, can be seen or understood to be the prince or leader of this fluid and dissolute nation, other than the discourse of that philosophy which judges pleasure to be the highest good —…

For these "eighteen years" of servitude also passed, and it is not recounted that "they cried out to the Lord" or were converted from their wickedness, but after eighteen years it is again said that: "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up for them a Savior, Ehud the son of Gera, the son of Gemini, a man ambidextrous." Behold what manner of man this is who is raised up to save Israel! He has nothing left-handed in himself, but has both hands as a right hand; for this is what is meant by "ambidextrous." Truly a worthy leader of the people and judge of the Church, who does nothing left-handed, whose "right hand knows not what his left hand does," who is right-handed on either side — right-handed in faith, right-handed in deeds — who has nothing of those who are placed "on the left," to whom it is said: "depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I know you not;…

"And they adored", it says, "strange gods, the gods of the nations who were round about them, and they provoked the Lord to anger". See how much sins accomplish, that we who sin are said to provoke to anger him in whom there is not only no affection of anger, but not even any other passible movement. Truly he remains unchangeable in his nature and is never disturbed by the affections of anger; but I, through the things in which I transgress, decree anger for myself, just as the Apostle says, teaching this very thing: "but according to your hardness and impenitent heart you treasure up", he says, "for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each one according to his works".

After the death of Joshua the son of Nave [Nun] they forsook the God of their fathers and served idols, Baalim and Ashtaroth; and the Lord in anger delivered them up to the hands of plunderers, and they continued to be plundered by them and to be sold to their adversaries, and [they] could not at all stand before their enemies. Wherever they went forth, his hand was upon them for evil, and they were greatly distressed. And after this God sets judges, the same as our censors, over them. But not even these did they continue steadfastly to obey. So soon as one of the judges died, they proceeded to transgress more than their fathers had done by going after the gods of others and serving and worshiping them. Therefore the Lord was angry. "Since, indeed," he says, "this nation has transgressed my covenant which I established with their fathers and has not hearkened to my voice, I will not…

quotes.quote: (Judges 5:15) The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah. In Hebrew: the princes, that is, the teachers of the Law, were with Deborah to praise the Lord, and Barak followed in the footsteps of the age. It is to be understood that a certain part of them remained with Deborah to praise the Lord, and a part followed Barak to exhort and vanquish Sisera. Who, as if into a precipice, gave himself to danger. Barak, indeed, believing the words of the Lord, gave himself to danger, throwing himself into the torrent Kishon, pursuing and vanquishing the army of Sisera. For in this place a raging torrent is understood as the abyss. Ruben, on the other hand, is divided within himself, and a dispute of noble men is found. It is written in the Book of Judges against itself. For the voice of Deborah is heard, rebuking the tribe of Ephraim, because they did not obey the command of the Lord and did not go…

quotes.quote: (Judges 5:6) In the days of Sangar, the son of Anath, in the days of Jahel, the paths remained empty, and those who entered through them walked along crooked roads. The paths are said to have remained empty because during the time of Sangar, the leader of Israel, the paths had been taken over by enemies of Israel, and they did not dare to freely ascend to the house of the Lord to pray; instead, those who entered through them secretly ascended through crooked streets, out of fear of the enemies. Concerning which enemies Sangar is said to have not fully freed them (Judg. 3:31). But what is inserted a little above, in the days of Jahel, is to be understood, because when Sisara was killed by Jahel, the roads were opened, and they went into the house of the Lord without any fear, who previously went there by winding paths. quotes.quote: SINCE ABRAHAM WAS FORBIDDEN TO SACRIFICE HIS SON, WHY WAS JEPHTHAH NOT FORBIDDEN TO CARRY OUT THE SACRIFICE OF HIS DAUGHTER? (Gen. 22:11–12; Judg. 11)? — There is a great difference between Abraham’s case and Jephthah’s case. First, Abraham was legitimately born, whereas Jephthah was illegitimate, for he was the son of a prostitute. Next, Abraham was of excellent conduct, but Jephthah was a leader of bandits. Abraham was a righteous man, proven in temptation; in Jephthah, however, there is no testimony of righteousness. Abraham, therefore, was commanded to offer his son to God so that it might be shown to people how greatly Abraham trusted God, since at His command he did not hesitate even to kill his own son. For He who, contrary to worldly hope, could cause him to be born of a barren old woman, was clearly able, contrary to worldly reasoning, to raise him from the dead (Heb. 11:19).…
